name: Maya Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Go for it. I'm quite into all this, so you might get more than you bargained for.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on a three-person crew building decks, fences, garden rooms and pergolas, mostly for families in the newer estates outside town. I dig post holes, mix concrete, cut joists and screw down boards, and I'm learning to build the garden rooms properly. My favourite bit is handing over a finished deck and watching the kids run straight onto it. The worst bit is digging post holes in clay when it's been raining for a week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you're into all this. In what way?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use AI every day. I do the boss's quotes on it now, I plan my week with it, and I asked it to explain load spans for a deck, which saved me a telling-off. I live with my partner Daniel, he's an apprentice electrician, and we've got maybe three weeks of savings. I'd like my own business one day, my grandad ran a joinery shop and I think it's in the blood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I still find it useful, even if it's not the revolution. At work I'd keep using it for quotes. Online I'd say it's a tool, use it like a tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means my plans stay the same, just slower. Decks and fences depend on people having spare money, so if things get tight, we're the first thing families cut. The boss already had a quiet February last year and sent me home for two weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for quotes and scheduling, because it saves the boss an evening a week. I'd keep learning garden rooms, because they pay best. And I'd put a little aside each month toward my own tools, a mitre saw and a post-hole auger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit impatient to get going on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said decks are the first thing families cut. How did last February feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scary. Two weeks with no pay, and Daniel's apprentice wage barely covers his half of the rent. My mum dropped round a bag of shopping and I nearly cried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to change, if AI stays small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want small businesses to have it easier, less red tape, cheaper insurance. Then people like me could start up sooner. I don't want a handout, I want a fair start.

I'd tell people online it's a **tool**, so use it like one.
think: **Decks and fences** are the first thing families cut when money is tight.
Her plans stay the same, just **slower**.
do: Keep doing the boss's **quotes and scheduling** with AI.
Keep learning **garden rooms**, which pay best.
Save toward a **mitre saw** and post-hole auger.
feel: **Mostly fine**, but **impatient** to start her own business.
S0.quote: Decks and fences depend on people having spare money, so if things get tight, we're the first thing families cut.
fieldNote: Her work depends on **household spending**, not AI.

She wants **less red tape**, not handouts.
She's already the crew's **AI user**, doing the boss's quotes.

steps.text: Do the boss's quotes and weekly schedule with AI
Learn to build garden rooms from start to finish
Save monthly toward a mitre saw and post-hole auger

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for small businesses if they move fast. At work I'd say let me run the quotes and booking side completely. Online I'd post how I'm using it, because other tradespeople ask me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's a chance. If AI does the quotes, bookings and ordering, a small crew can run with no office at all. That's exactly what I need to start my own business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up the boss's online booking with AI this year, so he sees I'm worth more. I'd start doing small fence jobs on Saturdays under my own name. And I'd keep saving for tools, maybe four hundred by summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. A bit nervous about the money, but mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The boss's wife, who does his paperwork from the kitchen table. If I set up the AI booking, I'm kind of taking her job. I'd want to talk to her first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got three weeks of savings. Is starting a business sensible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet, no, that's why it's Saturdays. Daniel would say wait until he qualifies, and he's right. But I'd rather start small than not at all.

Do small **Saturday fence jobs** under her own name.
Save **four hundred** for tools by summer.

steps.text: Set up AI online booking for her boss's decking crew

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say everyone in a trade needs to get ready, now. At work I'd tell the boss we've got about three years before robots build decks. Online I'd share what I'm doing to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm scared. The paperwork side is gone in 2028, which is the bit I'm good at. Then by 2031 robots can dig post holes and screw down boards, and that's the rest of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2028 I'd use AI to get as many garden-room jobs as I can, fast, under my own name. I'd save every penny for three years. And Daniel and I would talk about whether to put off the wedding, which my nan would hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like being handed a head start and then told the race is shorter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why put off the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because we'd need every penny for a cushion, not a party. My nan says you don't wait on God's timing for money. But she didn't have robots coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do once robots arrive in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe be the person who sells and installs them for garden builds, because I know the work. Or run a crew of robots with a few people for the fiddly bits. I honestly don't know if that job will exist.

say: I'd say everyone in a trade needs to **get ready now**.
I'd tell the boss we have **three years** before robots build decks.
think: The **paperwork side** she's good at goes in 2028.
By **2031** robots dig post holes and screw down boards too.
do: Win as many **garden-room jobs** as possible under her own name.
Discuss **putting off the wedding** with her partner.
feel: Like a **head start** cut short by a **shorter race**.
S2.quote: The paperwork side is gone in 2028, which is the bit I'm good at.
fieldNote: She's hit **twice**: her desk skills first, then her hands-on work.
Delaying the **wedding** clashes with her grandmother's faith.
She'd try to **sell or run robots** but doubts the job exists.
She still has **plans**, so anxious rather than alarmed.

steps.text: Win garden-room jobs under her own name before 2031
Save every spare pound for three years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build something. At work I'd tell the boss to modernise now. Online I'd post my plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, eight years until robots is time to build a real business. I could have my own crew by 2031, use AI for all the office side, and then decide whether to buy robots myself. I'd be on the buying side of the robots rather than being replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd register as a sole trader and do Saturday jobs. I'd get my carpentry papers at night school so customers trust me. And I'd save for a van, second-hand, maybe three thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful. A bit anxious about doing too much at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Daniel think about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd want in once he qualifies, so we'd do decks and garden rooms with lighting. That's a nice little family business, like my grandad's shop. Nan would love it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Burning out, honestly. Working weekdays for the boss and weekends for myself. I'd have to watch that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is great for anyone who's willing to work. At work I'd say let's grow. Online I'd say small trades should start planning now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirteen years until robots, I'd be forty with a proper business. With ten years, robots would be something I buy to help, not something that takes my job. I think it's good for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year: sole trader, papers, Saturday jobs, AI doing my bookings and quotes. Daniel qualifies in two years and joins me. We'd get married next year as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Genuinely good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said genuinely good, but you've got three weeks of savings. Is that fair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. The money's thin now, but with ten years I can fix that slowly. It's the short scenarios that scare me, not this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your grandad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say about time a woman in this family ran the shop. And then he'd ask why I'm not using proper oak.

I'd urge **small trades** to start planning now.

Robots would be something she **buys to help**, not a threat.
do: Run as a sole trader with **AI doing** bookings and quotes.
Bring her partner into the business once he **qualifies**.
S4.quote: With ten years, robots would be something I buy to help, not something that takes my job.
fieldNote: She's **calm** because the long runway fits her business plans.
She admits **thin savings** but trusts time to fix them.
Her **grandad's joinery shop** shapes her ambition.
She keeps **family plans** on schedule in this world.

steps.text: Run Saturday deck and garden-room jobs as a sole trader
Use AI for all her bookings and quotes
Marry her partner next year as planned

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My paperwork skills go first and then my hands-on ones, and I'd have three years to build a business from nothing. What would help is cheaper insurance and less red tape for new sole traders, and a small start-up loan for tools and a van.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my nan. She thinks all this is a test of faith, and she might be right. Either way, she's the one who'd feed us if it went wrong.

headlineQuote: I don't want a handout, I want a fair start.
portrait: Maya is **27**, a junior on a **decking and garden-room** crew, with about three weeks saved.
She uses **AI daily** and already runs her boss's quotes on it.
She's **traditional** on family and faith and wants less red tape, not handouts.
AGI by **2028** worries her because both her **desk and hands-on** skills go.
With ten years she's **calm**, planning her own business with her electrician partner.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, losing her paperwork and then her hands-on skills.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheaper insurance**, less red tape and a small **start-up loan** for tools.
